job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Iris Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my grandmother in Monterrey, and the day starts with Mass at seven when I can make it, then breakfast with the family. I send applications until noon and then go to my uncle's workshop, where I help rewire motors for a small fee. In the evenings I plan things for my wedding with my fiancé, Mateo. It's a good home, but I'm restless about not having a real job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what was the internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied electrical engineering at the Tec in Monterrey and finished with a good result. I did a two-month internship at a substation with the state power company, helping a crew check relays and update the paper logs. A supervisor named Ing. Rojas praised my care, but they said no graduate posts until next year. I have some debt, about six weeks of savings, and my parents say they'll help, but I don't like to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it means people still matter in a workplace. I'd tell my friends that a firm is built on people and trust, not on gadgets. I don't use those tools, and I don't plan to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still worried because jobs for new engineers in Monterrey come and go, and many go to people whose cousin works there. Mateo and I wanted to marry next June, and without my salary we'd have to push it back. It isn't AI that stands in my way, it's that nobody has opened a door yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending applications to the power company, factories and consultancies, around fifteen a month. I'd also go to church groups and family gatherings and tell people I'm looking, because here jobs come through people you know. I'd keep helping my uncle with motors, since it earns a bit and keeps my hands busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and a bit tired. I pray and I try not to complain, because my parents have given me a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you tell people at church you're looking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's how things get done here, you ask and someone's cousin knows someone at the plant. My father got his job at the bakery supply firm by asking around, and I'm not too proud to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving the wedding mean for you and Mateo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean another year of waiting, and my grandmother would be sad because she wants to see it. Mateo is patient, he's a mechanic and he understands. But I'd feel I let down the family a little.

say: I'd say it's good, since a firm is built on **people and trust**, not gadgets.
I don't use those tools and don't plan to start.
think: Jobs for new engineers in Monterrey come and go, and many go to people with a **cousin inside**.
Without my salary, Mateo and I would have to push back our June wedding.
do: Send about **fifteen applications** a month to the power company, factories and consultancies.
Tell people at **church and family** gatherings that I'm looking.
Keep helping my uncle **rewire motors** for a small fee.
feel: Hopeful and a bit tired; I pray and try not to **complain**.
S0.quote: My father got his job at the bakery supply firm by asking around, and I'm not too proud to ask.
fieldNote: Anxiety is about the wedding date, family expectations and how jobs get filled locally.
Her trust in **people networks** is a practical view, not nostalgia.
She never links her worry to AI; she wants a door opened, not a new tool.

steps.text: Send fifteen applications a month to the power company and factories
Tell church and family I'm looking for engineering work
Rewire motors at my uncle's workshop for pay
Pay only the minimum on my student debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and families should prepare, but we shouldn't forget what keeps a community together. Planning and checking are on the card, and that's a lot of paperwork engineers do. I'd say people should work hard and learn a real trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid the junior desk jobs go first, like checking drawings and updating logs. At the substation I saw how much of the work was paperwork, and I could see a program doing it. The jobs with hands, like climbing a pole or testing a relay, last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for field roles, like maintenance and commissioning, where a person has to be on site. I'd ask Ing. Rojas about an apprenticeship with the power company, because I believe in learning by doing. I wouldn't touch the AI tools unless I had to, but I'd learn whatever the crew uses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and careful. I'd light a candle and keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't touch the tools unless you had to. What would make you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my boss said, this is how the job is done, I'd learn it. I don't oppose it, I just don't run after new things. My uncle waited three years to try a new meter, and then it saved him hours, so I'm not stubborn about it forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about people who do use them all the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of envy, honestly, and a bit of worry that they'll forget how to do things by hand. At the substation, the old crew chief could find a fault with a single ear. A program can't teach that.

say: I'd say it's a big change and families should prepare, but **community** still matters.
I'd tell people to work hard and learn a real trade.
think: Junior desk jobs like checking drawings and updating **logs** go first; I saw how much was paperwork.
Hands-on jobs like climbing a pole or testing a relay last longer.

Ask Ing. Rojas about an **apprenticeship** with the power company.

fieldNote: Her resistance to tools is slow, not total: she'd learn them when a boss asks.
She values **apprenticeship** and hands-on skill, which fits her traditional views.
Her sense of the substation's paperwork gives her a grounded view of what AI could replace.

steps.text: Ask Ing. Rojas about a power company apprenticeship
Apply for field maintenance and commissioning roles
Learn the crew's software only when my boss asks
Keep helping at my uncle's workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for families, and we need to look after one another. I'd say the churches and neighbourhoods must be ready to help, and I'd say employers should keep their people, not just cut them. I'd talk about it at the family table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened. If a machine does thinking work better and cheaper in two years, why would a power company hire me to check logs? Robots are three years away from the hands-on work, so maybe my hands could save me for a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work with my uncle full time, and I'd put the wedding on a small budget, with a Mass and a family lunch only. I'd stop my own spending, give up the gym and my phone upgrade, and ask my parents about staying at home longer. I'd also ask Ing. Rojas if they need people who can work on the lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, but I'd hold on to my faith. It's the one thing that doesn't depend on machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mateo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we don't need a big party, we need each other and a plan. He'd laugh and say we'll marry in a garden, and we'd probably cry a little. He's good at keeping me calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your parents, what would you want from them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To hear that we'll manage. My mother would put food on the table and my father would say work is dignity. I'd want that, even if it isn't a plan.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for families and we must look after one another.
I'd say employers should keep their people, not just cut them.
think: I'm frightened: why would a power company hire me to check logs if a machine does it **cheaper**?
Robots are three years away from hands-on work, so my hands may save me for a time.

Stop my own spending and stay at **home longer**.
Ask Ing. Rojas about work on the **power lines**.
feel: Afraid, but I'd hold on to my **faith**, which doesn't depend on machines.
S2.quote: We don't need a big party, we need each other and a plan.
fieldNote: Fear is concrete: she expects her paperwork-style entry job to disappear.
Her fallback is **hands-on work** with family, plus a smaller wedding.
Faith and her fiancé are her steadying forces, mentioned without prompting.

steps.text: Work full time at my uncle's workshop
Shrink the wedding to a Mass and family lunch
Give up extras and track every peso
Stay at my parents' home longer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people get serious. I'd tell the young to learn a trade or a field skill, and I'd tell firms to invest in apprentices. Churches and neighbourhoods can help, but work is what gives people dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious but there's a path. If I land a job on a crew in the next year, I'd have four years of practice before the thinking work is automated. And robots come a few years after, so there's room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first field job I could get, even with long hours, and stay put for several years. I'd save for the wedding and move it forward if I can. I'd also keep helping my uncle on Saturdays, since a second income helps and I like the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. It's slow and steady, which suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the first year's pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give a part to my parents for the house, then pay down my debt and put aside for the wedding. I'd buy nothing for myself for six months, not even new shoes. It sounds strict but it feels right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the thinking work goes faster than the card says?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd already be in the field, and that's where I'd want to be. I'd also tell my younger cousins to learn welding or electrical work, because those don't vanish overnight.

Work is what gives people dignity.
think: I'm anxious but there's a path: a crew job this year gives me four years of **practice**.
Robots come a few years later, so there's room.

Save for the **wedding** and give a part to my parents for the house.
Keep helping my uncle on **Saturdays** for a second income.
feel: Hopeful, in a **slow and steady** way that suits me.
S3.quote: I'd buy nothing for myself for six months, not even new shoes.
fieldNote: Five years suits her patient, loyal-to-employer pattern.
Her plans put **family** first: parents' house, the wedding, younger cousins' trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time, long enough to raise a family and still adapt. I'd tell young people to marry, work and learn a skill, and not to be afraid. I'd say the families that stay close will do better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm. In ten years I could be a senior technician, married, with two children. I'd keep an eye on what changes, but I wouldn't lose sleep over it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a stable job with the power company or a factory, study part time for a professional licence, and save for a small house. I'd marry Mateo in June as planned, if I have work. I'd stay with the church community, because we help each other when times are hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful. It feels like I'm allowed to live a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a normal life mean for you in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house with a small garden, children at school, my parents nearby, and a job I understand. I'd still help my uncle if he needed me. And I'd go to Mass on Sundays with the whole family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in those ten years you'd still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents getting old. They'd need care, and I'd want to be the one to give it. Technology can't replace the care my parents will need when they get old, and I hope nobody tries.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough to **raise a family** and still adapt.
I'd tell young people to marry, work and learn a skill without fear.
think: I'm calm: in ten years I could be a senior **technician**, married, with two children.
I'd watch what changes but wouldn't lose sleep now.
do: Take a stable job with the power company and study for a **professional licence**.
Save for a **small house** and marry Mateo in June if I have work.
Stay in the **church** community, where people help each other.
feel: Peaceful, as if I'm allowed to live a **normal life**.
S4.quote: Technology can't replace the care my parents will need when they get old, and I hope nobody tries.
fieldNote: Even in the easiest case, she names ageing parents as her real concern.

Uneasy rather than calm because her debt and the job search come first.

steps.text: Take a stable job and study for a professional licence
Save for a small house near my parents
Marry Mateo in June if I have work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to build a life. What would help is apprenticeships with real wages, employers who keep their people, and families and churches that look after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd tell other girls studying engineering. I'd say, be patient and don't take every shortcut. A good career is built on careful work, and I still believe that, even if the world changes.

headlineQuote: A good career is built on careful work, and I still believe that, even if the world changes.
portrait: Iris is an **electrical engineering** graduate in Monterrey, living with her parents and grandmother, with no offer yet.
She is engaged to Mateo, a mechanic, and her wedding date depends on getting her first salary.
She never uses AI tools and values apprenticeships, family networks and hands-on skill over new technology.
Her mood runs from anxious at most scenarios to **alarmed** at two years, and uneasy at ten.
She blames shortcuts and cost-cutting employers, and trusts faith, family and patient work.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case, because there'd be no time to build a life.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** with real wages and employers who keep their people.
Families and churches that look after each other.
